slides.text: Every major AI lab is now shipping agents that run unattended, with standing access to your inbox and accounts. One engineer's first test of OpenAI's version turned up **something worth pausing on** before anyone wires one to a real inbox.

Testing the agent's sandboxed browser against Gmail, one engineer found the connection wasn't going straight to Google. It came back with an **OpenAI-issued certificate** for gmail.com instead of Google's own.

Another developer in the discussion pointed out what that means: traffic inside the sandbox is being intercepted, and most browsers on Linux don't pin certificates, so the interception is **invisible to the agent, and to you.**
That's not automatically malicious. Vendors often inspect sandbox traffic for safety. But it means **the vendor can see everything the agent reads or sends,** including whatever's in that inbox.

panel.small: found inside the agent's own sandbox

slides.text: Not everyone in the thread was worried. One developer argued domain-specific always-on agents are genuinely useful: **they avoid overloading one model's context** and give each agent a clearer boundary of what it can touch.

Another engineer skipped the vendor product entirely. He built his own always-on agents in dedicated Unix accounts, wired straight into his own mailbox, running **on infrastructure he fully controls.**

A developer in the thread noted how fast the norms moved: months ago, the consensus was never give an agent read or write access to anything sensitive. Now people are wiring these into real inboxes **without checking what's happening on the wire.**

Before you give any agent standing access to your accounts, check its network path first: **is it intercepting your traffic, and where does that data go?** Building it yourself, on infrastructure you control, is still the safer default.
Have you checked what your AI agent's sandbox can actually see on the wire? **Tell me what you found,** and save this before you connect one to anything real.
